title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text: This course treats AI coding assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and similar) as professional tools: you will learn to use them effectively and critically, and you will also develop the individual fluency to program without them.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text:
Why this policy
Statistical programmers now work alongside AI tools daily. Banning them would prepare you for a world that no longer exists; letting them do your thinking would leave you unable to catch their mistakes, and they make plenty. The course therefore teaches the skill that actually matters: directing AI tools and verifying their output. Week 8 is a dedicated workshop, and every week includes a short “AI corner” showing one good and one bad AI use for that week’s topic.
Free-tier AI tools are sufficient for all coursework; no paid subscriptions are required or expected.
Submitting AI-generated work you do not understand, using AI during a quiz, or omitting required disclosure is an academic-integrity violation.

if Traps to Avoid


Vector condition = error
sbp_vec <- c(120, 165, 190)
if (sbp_vec >= 140) { ... }
# Error: the condition has length > 1
if inspects one value; vectors need ifelse() (next!).

NA condition = error
x <- NA
if (x > 5) { ... }
# Error: missing value where
# TRUE/FALSE needed
Guard first: if (!is.na(x) && x > 5).

title: Week 8: Control Flow & Iteration
text:
Vectorized Decisions: ifelse()
ifelse(condition_vector, value_if_true, value_if_false) decides element by element:
sbp_vec <- c(120, 165, 190, 135)

ifelse(sbp_vec >= 140, "elevated", "normal")
#> "normal" "elevated" "elevated" "normal"
# Perfect inside mutate()
gm |>
  filter(year == 2008) |>
  mutate(le_group = ifelse(life_expectancy >= 75, "high", "lower"))

Many Categories: case_when()
Nested ifelse() calls get unreadable fast: dplyr::case_when() scales cleanly:
gm |>
  filter(year == 2008) |>
  mutate(bp_stage = case_when(
    child_mortality >= 100 ~ "very high",
    child_mortality >= 50  ~ "high",
    child_mortality >= 10  ~ "moderate",
    !is.na(child_mortality) ~ "low",
    TRUE ~ NA
  ))

Conditions are checked in order; first TRUE wins (like else if chains).
The final TRUE ~ ... is the catch-all “else”.

text:
The Accumulator Pattern
Build a result before the loop, fill it inside the loop:
# Cumulative case counts over an outbreak week
daily_cases <- c(3, 7, 12, 20, 31, 26, 18)

total_so_far <- numeric(length(daily_cases))  # pre-allocate!
running_total <- 0

for (i in seq_along(daily_cases)) {
  running_total <- running_total + daily_cases[i]
  total_so_far[i] <- running_total
}

total_so_far
#> 3 10 22 42 73 99 117






Tip


Pre-allocating with numeric(n) beats growing a vector with c() inside the loop: both cleaner and dramatically faster.

title: Week 8: Control Flow & Iteration
text:
Vectorize First, Loop Second
Most “loops” in R are already built in:



Loop version
Vectorized version




sum with accumulator
sum(x)


running total loop
cumsum(x)


elementwise transform loop
x * 2, log(x)


conditional relabel loop
ifelse(...)



Reach for a loop when steps depend on previous results (simulations, iterative algorithms) or when you must produce side effects (saving files, printing reports).

title: Week 8: Control Flow & Iteration
section: while: Repeat Until a Condition Fails
text:
while: Repeat Until a Condition Fails
Use when you don’t know in advance how many iterations you need:
# An intervention cuts weekly cases by 20%.
# How many weeks until fewer than 10 cases?
cases <- 200
weeks <- 0

while (cases >= 10) {
  cases <- cases * 0.8
  weeks <- weeks + 1
}

weeks    # 14
cases    # 8.8

title: Week 8: Control Flow & Iteration
text:
while Safety Rules


1. The condition must eventually fail
while (cases >= 10) {
  # forgot to update cases...
  weeks <- weeks + 1
}
# infinite loop! (Esc to stop)

2. Add a guard rail
while (cases >= 10 && weeks < 1000) {
  cases <- cases * 0.8
  weeks <- weeks + 1
}
A hard cap turns a hang into a debuggable result.








Warning


Every while body must move the state toward the exit condition.

Update the state inside the loop.

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
The Four Atomic Vector Types
In R, every element in an atomic vector must have the same type:


1. Numeric (Double)
Decimal numbers (default in R):
weights <- c(68.5, 72.0, 81.3)
typeof(weights) # "double"
2. Integer
Explicit whole numbers with L:
counts <- c(1L, 5L, 12L)
typeof(counts)  # "integer"

3. Character (Strings)
Text enclosed in quotes:
drugs <- c("aspirin", "statin", "placebo")
typeof(drugs)   # "character"
4. Logical (Booleans)
TRUE or FALSE (all caps):
adherent <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
typeof(adherent)# "logical"

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
The Type Hierarchy & Implicit Coercion
What happens when you mix different types in c(...)?
R silently converts everything to the least restrictive type:
\[\text{logical} \longrightarrow \text{integer} \longrightarrow \text{double} \longrightarrow \text{character}\]
# Logical to numeric (TRUE becomes 1, FALSE becomes 0)
sum(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE))  # Count how many TRUEs: 3
mean(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE))# Proportion of TRUEs: 0.5

# Numeric + Character becomes Character
c(10, 25, "missing")             # c("10", "25", "missing")






Pro-Tip for Health Data


mean(bp > 140, na.rm = TRUE) directly calculates the prevalence of hypertension by coercing logicals to 1s and 0s!

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Summary Statistics on Vectors
R has built-in vector aggregators:
chol <- c(185, 220, 240, 195, 210, NA)

length(chol)              # Total elements including NA (6)
sum(is.na(chol))          # Count missing values (1)
mean(chol, na.rm = TRUE)  # Arithmetic mean (212)
sd(chol, na.rm = TRUE)    # Standard deviation (20.8)
summary(chol)             # 5-number summary + Mean + NAs

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Sequences with : and seq()
Instead of typing numbers manually, generate sequences automatically:


The Colon Operator :
Consecutive integer sequences:
1:10
20:15    # Counts backward!
-3:3

The seq() Function
Flexible step sizes & lengths:
# By step size
seq(from = 0, to = 100, by = 20)
# Output: 0 20 40 60 80 100

# By total length
seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 5)
# Output: 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Repetition with rep()
The rep() function replicates values using times or each:


times (Pattern repetition)
Repeats the whole vector:
rep(c("A", "B"), times = 3)
# "A" "B" "A" "B" "A" "B"

# Unequal repetitions per element:
rep(c("Control", "Treated"), times = c(4, 2))
# "Control" "Control" "Control" "Control" "Treated" "Treated"

each (Element repetition)
Repeats each item before moving to next:
rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3)
# "A" "A" "A" "B" "B" "B"

# Combining both:
rep(c("Dose1", "Dose2"), each = 2, times = 2)
# "Dose1" "Dose1" "Dose2" "Dose2" "Dose1" "Dose1" "Dose2" "Dose2"

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Modulo Arithmetic %%
The modulo operator %% calculates the remainder of division:
14 %% 3   # 2  (14 = 4 * 3 + 2)
10 %% 2   # 0  (10 is even)






Common Applications in Data Science



Even numbers: x %% 2 == 0
Divisible by 5: x %% 5 == 0
Assigning participants to \(K\) rotating study groups: (1:N) %% K + 1

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
The Three Subsetting Methods
We extract elements using square brackets x[...]:
ages <- c(23, 45, 19, 31, 56, 42)


1. Positive Indices
Extract by position (1-indexed):
ages[1]        # 23
ages[c(1, 4)]  # 23 31
ages[2:4]      # 45 19 31

2. Negative Indices
Exclude specific positions:
ages[-1]       # All except 1st
ages[-c(2, 5)] # Drop 2nd & 5th
# ages[-2:4]   # ERROR! Use -(2:4)

3. Logical Subsetting
Extract where TRUE:
ages[ages > 40]
# 45 56 42

ages[ages >= 30 & ages <= 50]
# 45 31 42

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Logical Operators for Filtering
Combine conditions using element-wise logical operators:








Operator
Meaning
Example




&
Element-wise AND (both true)
(bmi > 25) & (age > 50)


\|
Element-wise OR (either true)
(status == "Severe") \| (fever == TRUE)


!
Logical NOT (inversion)
!(city %in% c("NY", "CA"))


%in%
Value matching (set membership)
id %in% confirmed_cases



sbp <- c(118, 142, 135, 160, 122)
stage2_htn <- sbp >= 140
sbp[stage2_htn]   # 142 160

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Modifying Vectors in Place (Mutation)
Use subsetting on the left side of <- to update specific elements:
scores <- c(88, -99, 95, -99, 72)

# Replace survey code -99 with NA:
scores[scores == -99] <- NA
scores
# 88 NA 95 NA 72

# Cap values at 90 (winsorizing):
scores[scores > 90 & !is.na(scores)] <- 90
scores
# 88 NA 90 NA 72

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Sorting, Ranking, and Ordering
Understanding the difference between sort(), rank(), and order():
vals <- c(30, 10, 50, 20)


sort(x)
Returns sorted values:
sort(vals)
# 10 20 30 50

sort(vals, decreasing = TRUE)
# 50 30 20 10

rank(x)
Returns rank position of each element:
rank(vals)
# 3 1 4 2
# (30 is 3rd, 10 is 1st, etc.)

order(x)
Returns indices that would sort x:
order(vals)
# 2 4 1 3
vals[order(vals)] # sorted!

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
Handling Ties in rank()
When numbers repeat, how should ranks be assigned?
scores <- c(80, 95, 80, 70)

rank(scores)                        # Default: average ranks (2.5 4.0 2.5 1.0)
rank(scores, ties.method = "first") # By appearance: (2 4 3 1)
rank(scores, ties.method = "min")   # Sports ranking: (2 4 2 1)






Tip


ties.method = "first" is essential for deterministic top-\(K\) rankings in data pipelines!

title: Week 2: Vectors & Subsetting
text:
AI Corner: Beware Vector Recycling!
When R operates on vectors of different lengths, it silently recycles the shorter one:


What R Does:
x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
y <- c(1, 2)
x + y
# Computes: 10+1, 20+2, 30+1, 40+2
# Output: 11 22 31 42

⚠️ The Danger with AI:

LLMs often generate code that accidentally recycles vectors when filtering or standardizing.
Always check length(x) == length(y) before element-wise operations!

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Why ggplot2?
Created by Hadley Wickham based on Leland Wilkinson's The Grammar of Graphics.

Declarative System: You describe what you want to see, not low-level drawing steps.
Layered Composition: Stack data, aesthetics, geometries, facets, and themes using +.
Publication Standard: Automatic legends, consistent scales, and reproducible output.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Base R vs. ggplot2


Base R (plot())

Fast for quick disposable sketches.
Pen-on-paper model (cannot easily modify earlier layers).
Hard to build multi-panel legends or faceting.


ggplot2 (library(ggplot2))

Object-oriented: store plots in variables (p <- ggplot(...)).
Effortless layering and faceting.
Standard across biomedical and epidemiology research.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
section: The 3 Core Components of Every Plot
text:
The 3 Core Components of Every Plot
\[  ext{Plot} =     ext{Data} +     ext{Aesthetic Mappings} +   ext{Geometric Layers}\]
ggplot(data = <DATA>, mapping = aes(<MAPPINGS>)) +
  <GEOM_FUNCTION>()

Data: A data.frame or tibble.
Aesthetics (aes()): Visual channels (\(x\), \(y\), color, size, shape, alpha).
Geometries (geom_*()): Visual representation (points, lines, bars, boxes).

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Building a Scatterplot: Step-by-Step
library(ggplot2)

# Step 1: Canvas (blank)
p <- ggplot(data = airquality, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone))

# Step 2: Add Points
p + geom_point()

# Step 3: Map a 3rd Variable to Color
p + geom_point(aes(color = factor(Month)), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8)

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Aesthetic Mapping vs. Setting Constants


Mapping Inside aes()
Connects a visual channel to a variable in your data:
# Color varies by Month
geom_point(aes(color = factor(Month)))

Setting Outside aes()
Sets a fixed constant for all observations:
# All points are navy and size 3
geom_point(color = "navy", size = 3, alpha = 0.7)








Tip


Never put fixed values inside aes() (e.g. aes(color = "blue")), as R will treat "blue" as a single-level categorical factor!

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Histograms (geom_histogram)
Visualizing a single continuous variable:
ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Temp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#3498db", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°F)", y = "Count")

Always test multiple binwidth values to avoid hiding peaks or creating artificial noise.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Density Curves (geom_density)
Smooth probability density estimates:
ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Temp, fill = factor(Month))) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°F)", y = "Density", fill = "Month")

Use alpha = 0.4 so overlapping sub-populations remain visible.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Boxplots (geom_boxplot)
Comparing distributions across categorical groups:
ggplot(airquality, aes(x = factor(Month), y = Ozone, fill = factor(Month))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = 1, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Ozone (ppb)")

Displays 5-number summary (Min, Q1, Median, Q3, Max) + outlier flags.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Boxplot + Jitter Overlay (geom_jitter)
Layering raw observations over boxplots reveals sample sizes and local clusters:
ggplot(airquality, aes(x = factor(Month), y = Ozone, fill = factor(Month))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5, color = "black")

Set outlier.shape = NA on the boxplot to prevent plotting outliers twice!

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Discrete Counts: geom_bar vs. geom_col


geom_bar() (Counts Rows)
When R calculates frequency for you:
# Data has raw individual rows
ggplot(airquality, aes(x = factor(Month))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue")

geom_col() (Pre-Summarized)
When data already has a numeric height column:
summary_df <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "West"),
  admissions = c(120, 340, 210)
)
ggplot(summary_df, aes(x = region, y = admissions)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen")

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Faceting with facet_wrap
Split complex multi-group data into clean sub-panels:
ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(color = "navy", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ Month, nrow = 1)

nrow = 1 aligns all panels in a single horizontal strip.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Controlling Facet Scales
By default, all subplots share the exact same axis limits (scales = "fixed").
# Independent y-axis limits for each panel:
facet_wrap(~ Month, scales = "free_y")

# Completely independent axes:
facet_wrap(~ Month, scales = "free")






Note


Use fixed scales when comparing absolute quantities; use free scales when comparing internal distribution shapes.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Informative Labels: labs()
Never leave raw column names on a presentation or report figure:
p_pub <- ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone, color = Wind)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black", linetype = "dashed", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Air Pollution Dynamics at LaGuardia Airport",
    subtitle = "Daily measurements of Ozone, Temperature, and Wind (May - Sep 1973)",
    x = "Maximum Daily Temperature (°F)",
    y = "Mean Ozone (ppb)",
    color = "Wind Speed\n(mph)",
    caption = "Source: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation"
  )

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Colorblind-Safe Scales & Themes


Viridis Palettes
p_pub + 
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis")

Perceptually uniform and legible in grayscale.


Clean Themes
p_pub + 
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Saving Figures: ggsave()
Save vector or high-resolution raster images for publications and reports:
ggsave(
  filename = "figures/figure1_ozone.png",
  plot = p_pub,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Spotting Truncated Baselines


❌ What AI Generated
# AI Prompt: "Bar chart of mortality rate"
ggplot(df, aes(x = year, y = rate)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(48, 52))

Truncating the \(y\)-axis baseline makes a 1% change look like a 500% surge!


✅ The Verified Rule

Length/Area geoms (geom_col, geom_bar) MUST start at 0.
For Overplotting: Use geom_jitter(), alpha < 0.5, or 2D density contours.
Color Accessibility: Always use colorblind-friendly scales (viridis).

summarize(): Collapse to One Row
Without grouping, summarize() collapses the whole table to a single row:
gm |>
  filter(year == 2008, !is.na(life_expectancy)) |>
  summarize(mean_le = mean(life_expectancy),

n() counts rows and takes no arguments.

text:
Why Joins? Data Lives in Pieces
Real public health data arrives as separate tables:

  patient_id = c("P1", "P2", "P3", "P4"),

inner_join() and anti_join()

text:
AI Corner: The Join That Quietly Doubled the Data
An AI assistant merged medication records onto patients:
patients |> left_join(prescriptions, by = "patient_id")
It ran without errors, but the patient count doubled: patients with multiple prescriptions now appear once per prescription, so every later average is silently weighted by prescription count.
Audit protocol for every join:

nrow() before and after: did the row count change? Why?
count(patient_id) |> filter(n > 1): are keys unique where you assumed?
anti_join() both directions: what failed to match?







Important


An AI can write a syntactically perfect join that is statistically wrong. The audit is your job.

text:
What is a Matrix?
A matrix is a 2-dimensional collection of elements of the same basic type (homogeneous), arranged in rows and columns.


Column-by-Column (Default)
m1 <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
m1
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6

Row-by-Row (byrow = TRUE)
m2 <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
m2
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6

Dimensions & Naming
# Check matrix dimensions
dim(m2)    # returns c(number_of_rows, number_of_columns)
nrow(m2)   # 2 rows
ncol(m2)   # 3 columns

# Adding Row and Column Names
rownames(m2) <- c("Hospital_A", "Hospital_B")
colnames(m2) <- c("ICU_Beds", "Ventilators", "Nurses")

2D Matrix Subsetting: [row, column]
Always remember: [row, column] (think “RC Cola” or “Roman Catholic”).
# 1. Single element: row 1, col 2
m2[1, 2]                     # 2

# 2. Entire row: leave column blank!

# 3. Entire column: leave row blank!
m2[, "ICU_Beds"]             # Hospital_A: 1, Hospital_B: 4

# 4. Submatrix: rows 1:2, columns 2:3
m2[1:2, 2:3]

# 5. Conditional replacement
m2[m2 < 3] <- 0

title: Week 3: Matrices, Lists, Data Frames & Data Import
text:
Why Do We Need Lists?
Vectors and matrices are homogeneous (all elements must be the exact same type).
In public health and clinical research, real records contain heterogeneous data: * Patient ID (character) * Demographics (character, numeric) * Blood pressure readings across multiple visits (numeric vector of length 5) * Lab test results (logical or nested sub-records)
A list is a flexible container whose elements can be of any type, length, or structure!

title: Week 3: Matrices, Lists, Data Frames & Data Import
text:
Creating & Inspecting Lists
patient_record <- list(
  id = "PT-84920",
  age = 54,
  smoker = FALSE,
  sbp_history = c(138, 142, 130, 128, 135),
  metadata = list(clinic = "Bellevue", enrolled = "2026-01-15")
)

# Inspect structure
str(patient_record)
List of 5
 $ id         : chr "PT-84920"
 $ age        : num 54
 $ smoker     : logi FALSE
 $ sbp_history: num [1:5] 138 142 130 128 135
 $ metadata   :List of 2
  ..$ clinic  : chr "Bellevue"
  ..$ enrolled: chr "2026-01-15"

title: Week 3: Matrices, Lists, Data Frames & Data Import
text:
The Crucial Difference: $ vs [[ ]] vs [ ]


1. $ or [[ ]] (Extract Contents)
Extracts the raw object inside the list compartment:
# Returns a NUMERIC VECTOR
patient_record$sbp_history
patient_record[["sbp_history"]]

# Now you can do math!
mean(patient_record$sbp_history) # 134.6

2. [ ] (Sub-list / Slice)
Returns a smaller list containing that compartment:
# Returns a LIST of length 1
sub_list <- patient_record[4]
typeof(sub_list) # "list"

# mean(sub_list) WILL FAIL!
# Lists cannot be averaged directly.








Tip


Think of a list as a train with cargo cars. [4] gives you the 4th car; [[4]] opens the car and gives you the cargo inside!

section: Data Frames: The Heart of Data Analysis
text:
Data Frames: The Heart of Data Analysis
A data frame is a list of equal-length vectors. Each column is a variable; each row is an observation.
# Creating a data frame
cohort <- data.frame(
  id = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05"),
  age = c(45, 62, 38, 71, 55),
  bmi = c(24.2, 31.0, 27.5, 29.8, 22.1),
  diabetes = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Inspecting
nrow(cohort)       # 5 observations
ncol(cohort)       # 4 variables
summary(cohort)    # Summary statistics for each column

title: Week 3: Matrices, Lists, Data Frames & Data Import
text:
Tibbles vs. Base Data Frames
A tibble (tibble::tibble()) is a modern data frame with refined behavior:


Base data.frame

Prints all rows and columns to console (can flood screen).
May coerce strings or drop dimensions unpredictably (df[, 1] becomes a vector).
Partial name matching (df$d might match df$diabetes).


tibble (library(tibble))

Clean printing: shows top 10 rows and variable types (<chr>, <dbl>, <lgl>).
Strict subsetting: tb[, 1] always stays a tibble.
Never coerces types or uses partial matching.

Subsetting & Filtering Data Frames
# 1. Accessing columns
cohort$bmi
cohort[["age"]]

# 2. Creating a new computed column
cohort$bmi_high <- cohort$bmi >= 30.0

# 3. Filtering rows by condition: df[condition, ]
seniors <- cohort[cohort$age >= 60, ]
seniors

# 4. Complex filtering: BMI > 25 AND non-diabetic
overweight_non_diab <- cohort[cohort$bmi > 25 & !cohort$diabetes, ]

title: Week 3: Matrices, Lists, Data Frames & Data Import
text:
The “Unknown” String Trap


❌ What AI Generated
# Prompt: "Read this blood pressure dataset from CSV"
bp_df <- read.csv("bp_data.csv")
mean(bp_df$systolic)
Output: [1] NA
Why? In the CSV, row 42 contained "Unknown". Base read.csv converted the entire systolic column to character!

✅ The Verified Fix
Always specify explicit na strings upon import:
library(readr)
bp_df <- read_csv(
  "bp_data.csv",
  na = c("", "NA", "Unknown", "Refused", "-99")
)

# Verify column types
spec(bp_df)
mean(bp_df$systolic, na.rm = TRUE)

Objects and Variable Assignment

# Using objects in expressions

Why Text Data Matters in Public Health
Free-text fields are everywhere, and they are messy:

Medication entries: "metformin 500mg BID", "METFORMIN 500 MG"

title: Week 7: Strings, Factors & Dates
text:
The Core stringr Verbs
meds <- c("metformin 500mg", "Lisinopril 10mg", "atorvastatin 20mg")









Function
Question
Example
Result




str_detect()
Does it match?
str_detect(meds, "statin")
F F T


str_count()
How many matches?
str_count(meds, "m")
3 0 1


str_extract()
What matched?
str_extract(meds, "\\d+mg")
"500mg" "10mg" "20mg"


str_replace()
Swap the match
str_replace(meds, "mg", " mg")
adds a space




str_to_lower(), str_to_upper(), str_trim(), str_length() handle cleanup basics.

text:
Regex: A Pattern Mini-Language



Pattern
Matches
Example




abc
literal text
"abc"


.
any single character
"a.c" matches "abc", "a2c"


\\d
any digit
"\\d\\d" matches "42"


\\w
letter, digit, or _



\\s
whitespace



[abc]
one of a, b, c
"[TF]" matches "T" or "F"


[0-9]
character range
same as \\d









Tip


In R strings you must double the backslash: the regex \d is typed "\\d".

title: Week 7: Strings, Factors & Dates
text:
Quantifiers & Anchors



Pattern
Meaning




x?
zero or one x


x*
zero or more


x+
one or more


x{3}
exactly three


^x
starts with x


x$
ends with x



codes <- c("NYC-BK-014", "BOS-DT-2", "NYC-QN-101", "nyc-si-77")

str_detect(codes, "^NYC")        # starts with NYC (case-sensitive!)
str_extract(codes, "\\d+$")      # trailing run of digits
str_detect(codes, "^[A-Z]{3}-")  # three capitals then a dash

Factors: Categorical Data Done Right
A factor stores a categorical variable with known, fixed levels:

                   levels = c("mild", "moderate", "severe"))

text:
Parsing Dates: Match the Order
library(lubridate)

ymd("2026-10-21")        # ISO style
mdy("10/21/2026")        # US style
dmy("21.10.2026")        # European style

visit_dates <- ymd(c("2026-01-15", "2026-03-02", "2026-10-21"))

Function name = the order of year, month, day in your raw text.
Parsing returns a true Date object: sortable, plottable, subtractable.

title: Week 7: Strings, Factors & Dates
text:
Date Components & Arithmetic
d <- ymd("2026-10-21")

year(d);  month(d);  day(d)
wday(d, label = TRUE)          # Wed

# Date arithmetic
d + days(30)                   # follow-up in 30 days
d - years(1)                   # one year ago
# Elapsed time between events
admit    <- ymd("2026-09-30")
discharge <- ymd("2026-10-21")
as.numeric(discharge - admit)   # length of stay in days

title: Week 7: Strings, Factors & Dates
text:
Intervals & Age Computation
dob   <- ymd("1985-06-15")
visit <- ymd("2026-10-21")

# Exact age in years at visit
age <- interval(dob, visit) / years(1)
floor(age)   # completed years: 41






Warning


Never compute age as (visit - dob) / 365.25 for clinical work; leap years and month lengths make interval() / years(1) the reliable idiom.

title: Week 7: Strings, Factors & Dates
text:
AI Corner: The Overconfident Regex
Asked to extract doses like "500mg", an AI wrote:
str_extract(rx, "[0-9]*mg")
Audit findings:

* means zero or more: the pattern happily matches a bare "mg" with no digits at all.
It misses "500 mg" (space before the unit) — silently returning NA.
Nobody tested edge cases.

# The audited version: at least one digit, optional space
str_extract(rx, "\\d+ ?mg")






Important


Regex from AI is a hypothesis, not an answer. Always test on: a normal case, a spaced case, and a should-NOT-match case.

Why Data Wrangling?
Analysts spend 50–80% of their time preparing data, not modeling it.

Raw public health data is messy: inconsistent units, irrelevant columns, impossible values, mixed granularities.
dplyr gives you a small vocabulary of verbs, each doing one thing well:




Verb
Question it answers




filter()
Which rows do I keep?


arrange()
In what order should rows appear?


select()
Which columns do I keep?


rename()
What should columns be called?


mutate()
What new columns do I need?

title: Week 5: Data Wrangling with dplyr & Pipes
text:
Today’s Dataset: Global Health (gm)
The gm dataset from the r02pro package tracks health indicators for world countries over time.
library(r02pro)
library(dplyr)

gm   # 65,531 rows x 33 columns

country, continent, year, population
life_expectancy, child_mortality, sugar, food_supply
smoking_male, smoking_female, GDP_per_capita, HDI

One row = one country in one year.

title: Week 5: Data Wrangling with dplyr & Pipes
text:
The Native Pipe |>
The pipe takes the object on its left and passes it as the first argument to the function on its right.


Nested (hard to read)
head(filter(gm, year == 2008), 3)
Read from the inside out. 😵

Piped (reads like a recipe)
gm |>
  filter(year == 2008) |>
  head(3)
Read top to bottom: take gm, then filter, then show 3 rows.








Tip


Type |> quickly with Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + M (after enabling the native pipe in RStudio: Tools → Global Options → Code → “Use native pipe operator”).

title: Week 5: Data Wrangling with dplyr & Pipes
text:
filter(): Keeping Rows That Match
filter() keeps rows where a logical condition is TRUE (the same logicals you built in Week 2!).
# Countries observed in 2008 with life expectancy over 80
gm |>
  filter(year == 2008, life_expectancy > 80)

Multiple conditions separated by commas are combined with AND (&).
Use | explicitly for OR:

# Rows from Africa OR Europe
gm |> filter(continent == "Africa" | continent == "Europe")

# Equivalent shortcut with %in%
gm |> filter(continent %in% c("Africa", "Europe"))

title: Week 5: Data Wrangling with dplyr & Pipes
text:
filter() and Missing Values
filter() silently drops rows where the condition evaluates to NA!
# Rows where sugar consumption exceeds 40 g/day
gm |> filter(sugar > 40)          # NA rows are gone, no warning

# Keep only rows where sugar was actually measured
gm |> filter(!is.na(sugar))

# Explicitly inspect the missing rows
gm |> filter(is.na(sugar))






Warning


Always ask: “How many rows did I lose, and why?” Check with nrow() before and after filtering.

Common dplyr Pitfalls


1. = vs == inside filter()
gm |> filter(year = 2008)   # ERROR
gm |> filter(year == 2008)  # correct

gm |> mutate(x = sugar * 7)
# printed... and discarded!

gm |> select("country")  # works, but
gm |> select(country)    # idiomatic

gm <- gm |> filter(year == 2008)

text:
AI Corner: Auditing an AI-Written Pipeline
An AI assistant produced this code for “average sugar consumption in Asia in 2008”:
gm %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarize(mean_sugar = mean(sugar))
Three audit findings:

It used verbs (group_by, summarize) we can’t verify yet, when a simple filter() + mean() answers the question.
It never filtered year == 2008, so it silently averages all years.
mean(sugar) returns NA because missing values were never handled.

# A verifiable Week-5 answer:
asia_sugar <- gm |> filter(year == 2008, continent == "Asia", !is.na(sugar))
mean(asia_sugar$sugar)






Important

R is one of the most popular programming languages in statistics and data science. This course will introduce various R programming topics, including R objects, data visualization, data import & export, data manipulation, creating functions and iterations for statistical simulations, and writing high-quality reports with R Markdown. This course equips graduate students with foundational and modern computing skills for reproducible public health data science.
